issue.issue_text: Whether courts have the power to determine if a particular rite or observance is regarded as essential by the tenets of a particular religion.

facts: The case involved a question about whether a specific religious practice was an essential rite protected under the Constitution of India.
law: Article 25 and 26 of the Constitution of India grant freedom of religion and the right for religious denominations to manage their own affairs in matters of religion, subject to public order, morality, and health.
application: The Court established that to determine what constitutes an essential part of a religion, it must primarily refer to the doctrines of that religion itself.
The Court cited precedent from two previous cases, *Ratilal Panachand Gandhi v. State of Bombay* and *Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj v. State of Rajasthan*.

In both of these prior cases, the Court had examined the specific tenets and practices of the religions in question to decide whether a particular observance was essential. By doing so, the Court established its role and power to make such a determination.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that courts have the power to determine whether a particular rite or observance is regarded as an essential part of a religion by examining the core tenets and doctrines of that religion itself, a practice supported by prior judicial precedent.

issue.issue_text: Whether every religious denomination or any section thereof has the right to manage its own affairs in matters of religion, subject to public order, morality and health, under Article 26 of the Constitution.

facts: The case involved the Ananda Marga, which the court identified as a socio-spiritual organization and a religious denomination within the Hindu religion.
The Ananda Marga claimed a fundamental right under Articles 25 and 26 to perform the Tandava dance in public streets and places.
law: Article 26 of the Constitution grants every religious denomination the right to manage its own affairs in matters of religion, but this right is explicitly subject to public order, morality, and health.

For an organization to be considered a 'religious denomination', it must be a collection of individuals with a system of beliefs for their spiritual well-being, a common organization, and a distinctive name.
The courts have the authority to determine whether a specific practice or rite is an 'essential' religious rite according to the tenets of a particular religion.

The right to freedom of religion under Articles 25 and 26 can be restricted by the State on grounds of public order, morality, and health, and the State can also regulate secular activities associated with religious practice.
application: The Court first applied its three-part test and determined that Ananda Marga qualified as a 'religious denomination' under Article 26.
The Court then examined the specific practice in question—the performance of the Tandava dance in public processions.
It concluded that performing the Tandava dance in public streets was not an essential religious rite of the Ananda Marga denomination.
Because the practice was not deemed an essential 'matter of religion', the Court held that it did not fall under the protection of Article 26.
This finding made it unnecessary for the Court to further consider whether a prohibition on the dance was justified in the interest of public order.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the principle that every religious denomination has a right under Article 26 to manage its own affairs in matters of religion, subject to public order, morality, and health. However, the Court clarified that this right only protects practices that are deemed essential religious rites. In this case, since the Tandava dance in public was found not to be an essential rite of the Ananda Marga denomination, the claim to a fundamental right to perform it was rejected.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A claim to a fundamental right under Articles 25 or 26 of the Constitution to perform a religious practice in public streets and public places will be rejected if that practice is not an essential and integral part of the religion.
obiter: Courts have the power to determine whether a particular rite or observance is regarded as essential by the tenets of a particular religion.

An order under Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is intended for emergent situations to prevent disorder and maintain public peace and is not meant to be permanent or semi-permanent in character.
A legislature is competent to pass a law permitting an authority to take anticipatory action or place restrictions on certain acts in an emergency to maintain public order.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The petitioner's claim to a fundamental right under Articles 25 or 26 to perform the Tandava dance in public streets and public places is rejected. Specifically, the petitioners have not established any legal right to carry fire torches, skulls, and daggers in public places or streets, as such acts implicate the interests and sense of security of other members of the public.
legal_tests_applied: The court first determines whether the claimed activity constitutes a fundamental right under Articles 25 or 26. If it does not, the court finds it unnecessary to then consider whether a state restriction on that activity is justified in the interest of public order.

The court balances the claimed right of religious expression against the interests of public order, considering factors such as the 'interests of other members of the public', the 'sense of security of the others', and the 'possibility of any attempt to retaliate or counter-act'.
why_appellant_lost: The court concluded that the petitioner's claim to have a fundamental right under Articles 25 or 26 to perform the Tandava dance in public streets and public places had to be rejected.

The court found that the petitioners failed to establish a legal right to carry 'fire torches, skulls and daggers' in public, as these specific actions are not protected rights when they involve the security and interests of the public.

Because the court found the activity was not a protected fundamental right, it deemed it unnecessary to examine the justification for the prohibitory order under the public order exception in Article 25.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was upheld because the court agreed that the state has the authority to regulate activities in public spaces that threaten public order and security.

The court's reasoning affirmed the state's duty to consider the impact of a procession on the public, stating, 'The interests of other members of the public are involved, the sense of security of the others is ·also involved.'
The court validated the state's concern for potential violence, noting that authorities must consider 'the question of the'!Jossibility of any attempt to retaliate or counter-act to the same'.
policy_considerations: The court drew a distinction between a permissible religious procession and one that includes elements that threaten public security, stating that 'brandishing fire torches or skulls or daggers in the public places including · streets cannot come under the. same category' as a peaceful demonstration.

The judgment reinforces the principle that the maintenance of public order is a primary duty of the state, which includes taking anticipatory action 'in an emergency where danger to public order is genuinely apprehended'.

The court acknowledged the difficulty in cases 'where the freedoln of religious convic• tions genuinely entertained by men come into conflict with the proper politicial attitude which is expected from citizens in matters of unity and solidarity of the State organization.'
